etymology: Anglo-Saxon leoht, not heavy — comparative degree, of less weight or burden.
biblical_def:
Make thou the grievous service of thy father, and his heavy yoke which he put upon us, lighter. My little finger shall be thicker than my father's loins. They are altogether lighter than vanity.

Lighter is the word Rehoboam's kingdom rises or falls on. The elders counsel him to make the people's yoke lighter and win lifelong service; the young men counsel the opposite, and their answer — my little finger shall be thicker than my father's loins — becomes the arrogance that splits the kingdom of Israel in two. The Psalter's lighter is theological rather than political: men of low degree are vanity, men of high degree are a lie, and set together in the balance they are altogether lighter than vanity, weightless before God regardless of worldly rank. Scripture's lighter therefore measures two very different scales at once: the burden a ruler chooses to lay on his people, and the weight every man actually carries before the LORD.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from LIGHT: not heavy; easy to be lifted or borne; comparative degree, of less weight or burden.
webster_full: LIGHT, a. Not heavy; having little weight.
Not burdensome; easy to be endured or performed.
Trifling; of small importance.
LIGHTER, a. Comparative of Light; of less weight, burden, or worth.
Applied to political burden (1 Kings) and to the moral weightlessness of every man before God (Psalm 62).
scriptures: Thy father made our yoke grievous: now therefore make thou the grievous service of thy father, and his heavy yoke which he put upon us, lighter, and we will serve thee.

And the young men that were grown up with him spake unto him, saying, Thus shalt thou speak unto this people that spake unto thee, saying, Thy father made our yoke heavy, but make thou it lighter unto us; thus shalt thou say unto them, My little finger shall be thicker than my father's loins.

And the young men that were brought up with him spake unto him, saying, Thus shalt thou answer the people that spake unto thee, saying, Thy father made our yoke heavy, but make thou it somewhat lighter for us; thus shalt thou say unto them, My little finger shall be thicker than my father's loins.
Psa 62:9
Surely men of low degree are vanity, and men of high degree are a lie: to be laid in the balance, they are altogether lighter than vanity.
corruption_summary: Modern leadership theory reads Rehoboam's failure purely as a public-relations blunder, missing that Scripture presents it as the LORD's own judgment dividing the kingdom according to prophecy (1 Kings 11:29-39).
corruption_paragraphs: A management-consulting reading of 1 Kings 12 treats the lighter-yoke episode as a case study in listening to constituents, with no reference to divine sovereignty. The text is explicit: the cause was from the LORD, that he might perform his saying, which the LORD spake by Ahijah the Shilonite unto Jeroboam.

The corrective is to read the political narrative theologically: rulers who will not make the yoke lighter for God's people answer to a higher throne than their own, and even a foolish young king's arrogance serves purposes he does not intend or perceive.
roots_summary: Psalm 62:9's lighter than vanity renders hevel (Heb.), a term for vapor or breath, the same word that gives Ecclesiastes its refrain vanity of vanities.
roots_lines: Lighter in 1 Kings 12 is the elders' counsel toward mercy the young king rejects.
Lighter in the young men's counsel becomes the arrogance that splits the kingdom.
The parallel account in 2 Chronicles 10 confirms the same divine hand at work.
Lighter in Psalm 62 measures every man's true weight before God, regardless of rank.
The Hebrew hevel behind lighter than vanity is the same breath-word behind Ecclesiastes' refrain.
usage: Make thou the heavy yoke lighter — the elders' counsel Rehoboam rejects.
My little finger shall be thicker than my father's loins — the arrogance that splits the kingdom.
Altogether lighter than vanity — every man's true weight before God, regardless of rank.

pos: verb (archaic 2nd person singular of lie, to recline)
etymology: Anglo-Saxon licgan, to lie down, recline — archaic second-person singular, thou liest.
biblical_def:
The land whereon thou liest, to thee will I give it. When thou liest down, and when thou risest up. Wherefore liest thou thus upon thy face?

Liest names the posture of rest, and in each case Scripture attaches a promise, a command, or a rebuke to that ordinary posture. The LORD's word to Jacob at Bethel comes to a man asleep with a stone for a pillow: the land whereon thou liest, to thee will I give it, covenant promise given at the lowest and most vulnerable moment of the patriarch's journey. Moses commands that God's words be spoken when thou liest down, and when thou risest up, framing every day's rest and rising with deliberate instruction of the children. Joshua's liest is sharpest of all: after the defeat at Ai, Joshua falls on his face before the ark, and the LORD's answer is not comfort but rebuke — wherefore liest thou thus upon thy face? — get up, for sin is in the camp and lying prostrate will not remove it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from LIE: to rest horizontally; to recline; archaic second-person singular form, thou liest.
webster_full: LIE, v.i. To rest or recline horizontally on any support.
To be situated, as a place or country.
To rest; to abide.
LIEST, v. Archaic second-person singular of Lie; thou reclinest, thou art situated.
Applied to covenant promise given in sleep (Genesis), daily instruction (Deuteronomy), and prophetic rebuke of misplaced posture (Joshua).
scriptures: And, behold, the LORD stood above it, and said, I am the LORD God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac: the land whereon thou liest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed;
Deu 6:7
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Jos 7:10
And the LORD said unto Joshua, Get thee up; wherefore liest thou thus upon thy face?
Pro 3:24
When thou liest down, thou shalt not be afraid: yea, thou shalt lie down, and thy sleep shall be sweet.
corruption_summary: A generic reading of Joshua 7:10 as simply telling Joshua to stop praying misses that the rebuke is specifically against passive lament substituting for the active removal of sin already named as the cause of defeat.
corruption_paragraphs: It is easy to read wherefore liest thou thus upon thy face as a general suspicion of prayer or lament in crisis. The text is far more specific: Israel hath sinned, and the LORD tells Joshua exactly what must be done — identify and remove the accursed thing — before intercession can properly continue.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that prayer and repentant action are not substitutes for one another; Joshua must rise from his face and lead Israel to deal with Achan's sin before the LORD's presence and blessing return.
roots_summary: Joshua 7:10's liest renders nophel (Heb.), fallen or prostrate, the same participle used of one fallen in defeat or in worship, requiring context to distinguish which.
roots_lines: Liest in Genesis 28 attaches covenant promise to Jacob's lowest, most vulnerable moment.
Liest in Deuteronomy 6 frames the whole day, lying down and rising, with instruction in the law.
Liest in Joshua 7 is prostration that must give way to active obedience.
Liest in Proverbs 3 promises undisturbed rest to the one who keeps wisdom.
The same Hebrew participle for lying prostrate applies to both defeat and worship, context alone distinguishing them.
usage: The land whereon thou liest, to thee will I give it — covenant promise given to a sleeping man.
When thou liest down, and when thou risest up — the law taught through the whole rhythm of the day.
Wherefore liest thou thus upon thy face? — rebuke against lament substituting for obedience.

pos: verb (archaic 2nd person singular past of call)
etymology: Anglo-Saxon ceallian, to call, summon — archaic second-person singular past tense, thou calledst.
biblical_def:
Why hast thou served us thus, that thou calledst us not. For thou calledst me. Thou calledst in trouble, and I delivered thee. Thou calledst to remembrance the lewdness of thy youth.

Calledst is Scripture's word for a summons remembered, whether the summons was given, withheld, or answered by God Himself. Ephraim's grievance against Gideon — that thou calledst us not — nearly turns Israel's deliverance into civil war, until Gideon's soft answer turns away wrath. Young Samuel's for thou calledst me, repeated three times in the dark before Eli understands what is happening, marks the first stirring of prophetic ministry in a boy who does not yet know the LORD's voice. Psalm 81 turns calledst toward covenant memory: thou calledst in trouble, and I delivered thee, God recalling His own past faithfulness as grounds for present obedience. Ezekiel's use is darkest of all — Jerusalem calledst to remembrance the lewdness of her youth — memory itself indicted as complicity in ongoing sin.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from CALL: to summon; to name; to invoke; archaic second-person singular past, thou calledst.
webster_full: CALL, v.t. To summon; to command or request to come or do something.
To name; to denominate.
To invoke; to appeal to.
CALLEDST, v. Archaic second-person singular past of Call; thou didst summon, name, or invoke.
Applied to a summons given (Judges), a summons received (1 Samuel), covenant deliverance recalled (Psalm 81), and sin recalled (Ezekiel).
scriptures: Jdg 8:1
And the men of Ephraim said unto him, Why hast thou served us thus, that thou calledst us not, when thou wentest to fight with the Midianites? And they did chide with him sharply.
And he ran unto Eli, and said, Here am I; for thou calledst me. And he said, I called not; lie down again. And he went and lay down.
Psa 81:7
Thou calledst in trouble, and I delivered thee; I answered thee in the secret place of thunder: I proved thee at the waters of Meribah. Selah.
Thus thou calledst to remembrance the lewdness of thy youth, in bruising thy teats by the Egyptians for the paps of thy youth.
corruption_summary: A therapeutic reading of memory as automatically healing ignores Ezekiel 23:21, where calling sin to remembrance is itself named a continuing act of unfaithfulness, not neutral recollection.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern therapeutic frameworks often treat remembering suffering and past affliction as inherently curative in itself. Ezekiel's calledst to remembrance describes the opposite: Jerusalem's dwelling on her former sins is presented as nostalgic complicity, a heart still drawn to what it ought to have forsaken.

The corrective is Paul's own pattern in Philippians 3:13 — forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before — memory of sin rightly used drives repentance and gratitude, not renewed attachment to the sin itself.
roots_summary: Psalm 81:7's calledst renders qara' (Heb.), to call or cry out, the same verb used throughout the Psalter for covenant prayer in distress.
roots_lines: Calledst in Judges 8 names a grievance that nearly turns deliverance into civil war.
Calledst in 1 Samuel 3 marks the first stirring of Samuel's prophetic call.
Calledst in Psalm 81 recalls God's own past deliverance as grounds for present obedience.
Calledst in Ezekiel 23 indicts memory itself as complicity in ongoing sin.
The Hebrew qara' behind covenant calledst runs throughout the Psalter's language of prayer in distress.
usage: Thou calledst us not — Ephraim's grievance nearly turning deliverance into civil war.
For thou calledst me — young Samuel's first, misunderstood encounter with the LORD's voice.
Thou calledst in trouble, and I delivered thee — covenant faithfulness recalled as grounds for obedience.

pos: verb (archaic 2nd person singular past of command)
etymology: Latin mandare, to entrust, order, via Old French comander — archaic second-person singular past, thou commandedst.
biblical_def:
The commandments... which thou commandedst thy servant Moses. The word that thou commandedst thy servant Moses. Commandedst them precepts, statutes, and laws. Nothing of all that thou commandedst them to do.

Commandedst belongs almost entirely to confession, the word believers use when admitting that God's clear word was disregarded. Nehemiah's prayer repeats it twice within two verses, laying Israel's exile squarely on having dealt very corruptly against the commandments, statutes, and judgments which thou commandedst thy servant Moses — no ambiguity about what was required is allowed to soften the confession. Nehemiah 9 widens the charge across the whole wilderness generation: precepts, statutes, and laws given by the hand of Moses, all commandedst, all eventually disobeyed. Jeremiah's usage in his own great confession is the most sweeping: they have done nothing of all that thou commandedst them to do, a totalizing indictment answered, remarkably, by the promise of a new covenant later in the same book.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from COMMAND: to order; to direct with authority; archaic second-person singular past, thou commandedst.
webster_full: COMMAND, v.t. To order; to direct authoritatively; to charge.
To have or exercise supreme power or authority over.
To require, as a duty.
COMMANDEDST, v. Archaic second-person singular past of Command; thou didst order or require.
Used almost exclusively in confession, acknowledging what God required and Israel failed to keep.
scriptures: Neh 1:7
We have dealt very corruptly against thee, and have not kept the commandments, nor the statutes, nor the judgments, which thou commandedst thy servant Moses.
Neh 1:8
Remember, I beseech thee, the word that thou commandedst thy servant Moses, saying, If ye transgress, I will scatter you abroad among the nations:
Neh 9:14
And madest known unto them thy holy sabbath, and commandedst them precepts, statutes, and laws, by the hand of Moses thy servant:

And they came in, and possessed it; but they obeyed not thy voice, neither walked in thy law; they have done nothing of all that thou commandedst them to do: therefore thou hast caused all this evil to come upon them:
corruption_summary: Modern minimizing of sin as mere mistake or shortfall softens confessions like Nehemiah's and Jeremiah's, which instead name total, deliberate disregard of what God plainly commandedst.
corruption_paragraphs: A therapeutic vocabulary of growth areas or missed opportunities cannot bear the weight of Jeremiah 32:23's confession: nothing of all that thou commandedst them to do. The prayer does not soften the charge to make repentance easier; it intensifies the charge because only an honest diagnosis produces real repentance.

The corrective is the pattern both prayers model: specific, unflinching confession of what God commanded and what was actually done, followed immediately by appeal to God's own covenant mercy — Nehemiah to God's promise of regathering, Jeremiah to the new covenant already being announced in the same book.
roots_summary: Nehemiah's commandedst renders tsivvah (Heb.), to command or charge, the same root behind mitzvah, commandment, the ordinary Hebrew word for the law given through Moses.
roots_lines: Commandedst in Nehemiah 1 grounds a confession of exile in specific, named disobedience.
Commandedst in Nehemiah 9 widens the charge across the whole wilderness generation.
Commandedst in Jeremiah 32 is the most total indictment of the four occurrences.
The Hebrew tsivvah behind commandedst is the same root behind mitzvah, commandment.
In every instance, commandedst frames confession, not merely historical record.
usage: The commandments... which thou commandedst thy servant Moses — Nehemiah's specific confession of exile's cause.
Commandedst them precepts, statutes, and laws — the wilderness generation's received and broken law.
Nothing of all that thou commandedst them to do — Jeremiah's total indictment before the promise of a new covenant.

pos: verb (archaic 2nd person singular past of send)
etymology: Anglo-Saxon sendan, to send, dispatch — archaic second-person singular past, thou sentest.
biblical_def:
Thou sentest forth thy wrath, which consumed them as stubble. Whither thou sentest us. Spake I not also to thy messengers which thou sentest unto me. The things which thou sentest to me for.

Sentest tracks something dispatched — wrath, spies, messengers, timber — back to the one who sent it, and Scripture uses the word to fix responsibility precisely where it belongs. Moses' song credits the LORD directly: thou sentest forth thy wrath, which consumed them as stubble, no secondary cause allowed to obscure the source of Egypt's destruction. The spies report to Moses using his own commission as their credential: the land whither thou sentest us, their whole mission authorized and defined by the one who sent it. Balaam repeats sentest twice to Balak's messengers, precise about the chain of command he is answerable within even as he resists using it for cursing Israel. Hiram's sentest to Solomon closes the pattern in ordinary commerce: a king's sent request for timber, honored as a matter of covenant friendship between two kingdoms.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SEND: to dispatch; to cause to go; archaic second-person singular past, thou sentest.
webster_full: SEND, v.t. To cause to go; to dispatch from one place to another.
To commission; to delegate with a message or errand.
To cause to be conveyed; to transmit.
SENTEST, v. Archaic second-person singular past of Send; thou didst dispatch or commission.
Applied to divine wrath dispatched (Exodus), a commissioned mission (Numbers), a chain of command (Balaam), and covenant commerce (1 Kings).
scriptures: Exo 15:7
And in the greatness of thine excellency thou hast overthrown them that rose up against thee: thou sentest forth thy wrath, which consumed them as stubble.
And they told him, and said, We came unto the land whither thou sentest us, and surely it floweth with milk and honey; and this is the fruit of it.
And Balaam said unto Balak, Spake I not also to thy messengers which thou sentest unto me, saying,
And Hiram sent to Solomon, saying, I have considered the things which thou sentest to me for: and I will do all thy desire concerning timber of cedar, and concerning timber of fir.
corruption_summary: Reading the exodus plagues as ancient natural disasters loosely attributed to God removes exactly what Exodus 15:7 insists on: thou sentest forth thy wrath as a direct, personal, first-cause divine action.
corruption_paragraphs: Naturalistic retellings of the Red Sea deliverance sometimes credit favorable winds or coincidental timing, with divine involvement reduced to interpretation laid over natural events. Moses' song will not permit the distance: thou sentest forth thy wrath is the LORD's own direct action, not providence discovered after the fact.

The corrective is to let the song's own theology stand: the LORD is a man of war, and the destruction of Pharaoh's host is His sent wrath, not a naturalistic coincidence that faith merely interprets religiously.
roots_summary: Exodus 15:7's sentest renders shalach (Heb.), to send forth, the same verb behind shaliach, one sent — an apostle — the root later applied to Christ's own commissioned messengers.
roots_lines: Sentest in Exodus 15 attributes the plagues and the sea's destruction directly to God, no secondary cause.
Sentest in Numbers 13 authorizes the spies' mission by Moses' own commission.
Sentest in Balaam's speech traces a precise chain of command he cannot escape.
Sentest in 1 Kings closes the pattern in ordinary covenant commerce between kingdoms.
The Hebrew shalach behind sentest is the same root that later gives apostle, one sent.
usage: Thou sentest forth thy wrath, which consumed them as stubble — direct divine action at the Red Sea.
The land whither thou sentest us — the spies' mission authorized by Moses' commission.
The things which thou sentest to me for — covenant commerce between Hiram and Solomon.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon agan, to have, own, owe — archaic second-person singular, thou owest.
biblical_def:
Pay me that thou owest. How much owest thou unto my lord? And how much owest thou? How thou owest unto me even thine own self besides.

Owest turns debt into confrontation in every place it appears, and the confrontations are pointed in opposite directions. The unforgiving servant, freshly released from an unpayable debt, seizes a fellow servant by the throat demanding pay me that thou owest — the same word he had just heard mercifully waived, now weaponized against another. The unjust steward's master asks the same question of debtors twice in Luke 16, but there the questioning exposes shrewdness rather than cruelty, the steward reducing bills he has no right to reduce to secure his own future. Paul's owest in Philemon inverts the whole pattern into gospel logic: whatever Onesimus owes, charge it to Paul's own account — albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides, Philemon's very conversion traced to Paul, a debt no bill could calculate.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from OWE: to be indebted; to be obliged to pay or repay; archaic second-person singular, thou owest.
webster_full: OWE, v.t. To be indebted to; to be obliged to pay.
To be obliged to ascribe or attribute, as an effect to a cause.
To have or possess by right, formerly.
OWEST, v. Archaic second-person singular of Owe; thou art indebted.
Applied to unforgiven debt weaponized (Matthew), shrewd debt reduction (Luke), and gospel debt absorbed by another (Philemon).
scriptures: But the same servant went out, and found one of his fellowservants, which owed him an hundred pence: and he laid hands on him, and took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest.
Luk 16:5
So he called every one of his lord's debtors unto him, and said unto the first, How much owest thou unto my lord?
Luk 16:7
Then said he to another, And how much owest thou? And he said, An hundred measures of wheat. And he said unto him, Take thy bill, and write fourscore.
Phm 1:19
I Paul have written it with mine own hand, I will repay it: albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides.
corruption_summary: A therapeutic reading of the unforgiving servant reduces the parable to generic advice about kindness, missing that Christ ties it explicitly to the doctrine of forgiveness among believers as a condition of ongoing fellowship with the Father.
corruption_paragraphs: Softened into a lesson about being nice, the parable of Matthew 18 loses its edge: the servant's crime is not rudeness but demanding what he himself had just been forgiven a thousand times over, and Christ's application is severe — so likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses.

The corrective is to hold the parable's full weight: forgiven debt that produces no forgiving heart exposes a debt never truly received as grace, and Philemon's owest unto me even thine own self shows the proper alternative — gospel debt absorbed voluntarily by one who has himself been forgiven much.
roots_summary: Philemon's owest renders prosopheileis (προσοφείλεις), you owe besides or in addition, Paul's deliberate wordplay building on the ordinary debt-word used just before it.
roots_lines: Owest in Matthew 18 exposes a forgiven debtor weaponizing debt against another.
Owest in Luke 16 belongs to a steward reducing bills he has no right to reduce.
Owest in Philemon inverts the pattern: Paul absorbs another man's debt voluntarily.
Paul's Greek wordplay in Philemon builds directly on the ordinary debt-term for owe.
In each case, owest exposes the true state of a heart toward mercy already received.
usage: Pay me that thou owest — the unforgiving servant's cruelty toward a fellow debtor.
How much owest thou unto my lord? — the unjust steward's shrewd reduction of bills.
How thou owest unto me even thine own self — Paul absorbing Onesimus's debt in Philemon.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon hire, possessive form of heo, she — belonging to her.
biblical_def:
If the firstborn son be hers that was hated. Restore all that was hers, and all the fruits of the field. As though they were not hers.

Hers marks legal or maternal claim in each of its uses, and every instance concerns a woman whose rightful claim is at risk of being overridden. Moses' law in Deuteronomy protects the unloved wife's firstborn son, hers that was hated, from being disinherited in favor of a favored wife's son — birthright determined by birth order, not by the father's preference. The Shunammite woman's restored property — all that was hers — comes only after Gehazi's intervention forces the king's hand, Elisha's earlier kindness to her finally paying out in full during famine and exile. Job's most severe image inverts the pattern entirely: the ostrich, hardened against her young ones, treats them as though they were not hers, a mother's natural claim on her offspring deliberately, almost cruelly, suspended by the Creator's own design.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from HER: possessive pronoun; belonging to her; used absolutely without a following noun.
webster_full: HER, pron. The objective and possessive case of She.
HERS, pron. The absolute possessive of She; used without a following noun, as, the field is hers.
Distinguished from her (adjective) in that hers stands alone, the possessed thing understood.
Applied in Scripture to inheritance rights (Deuteronomy), restored property (2 Kings), and a mother's claim on her young (Job).
In each instance the word marks a claim of ownership or right that is contested or at risk.
scriptures: If a man have two wives, one beloved, and another hated, and they have born him children, both the beloved and the hated; and if the firstborn son be hers that was hated:

And when the king asked the woman, she told him. So the king appointed unto her a certain officer, saying, Restore all that was hers, and all the fruits of the field since the day that she left the land, even until now.
She is hardened against her young ones, as though they were not hers: her labour is in vain without fear;
corruption_summary: Modern inheritance disputes are often settled by sentiment or preference alone; Deuteronomy 21:15-17 stands against exactly this, protecting an unloved wife's firstborn son by objective law regardless of the father's personal feeling.
corruption_paragraphs: A culture that prizes personal preference above all else struggles with a law that overrides a father's evident favoritism by fixed birthright rule. Deuteronomy 21 will not let a husband's love for one wife disinherit the legitimate firstborn of another, whatever his private feelings.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that biblical justice often overrides sentiment with fixed, objective rule precisely to protect the vulnerable from a stronger party's shifting preference.
roots_summary: Job 39:16's as though they were not hers renders lo lah (Heb.), not hers, part of God's extended speech from the whirlwind naming the ostrich's strange, divinely-appointed lack of wisdom toward her own young.
roots_lines: Hers in Deuteronomy protects an unloved wife's firstborn by fixed law, not paternal sentiment.
Hers in 2 Kings is restored property, the fruit of Elisha's earlier kindness finally repaid.
Hers in Job describes a mother's claim deliberately suspended in the ostrich by God's own design.
The Job passage belongs to the LORD's extended speech from the whirlwind on creation's strange wisdom.
In each case hers names a claim of right that is contested, protected, or withheld by design.
usage: The firstborn son be hers that was hated — protected inheritance rights under Mosaic law.
Restore all that was hers — the Shunammite woman's property returned after famine.
As though they were not hers — the ostrich's strange, God-appointed lack of maternal instinct.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon nigontynda, ordinal of nineteen — the number following eighteenth, preceding twentieth.
biblical_def:
The nineteenth to Pethahiah, the twentieth to Jehezekel. Which is the nineteenth year of king Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon.

Nineteenth appears in two very different registers of Scripture: the meticulous casting of lots for temple service, and the exact dating of Jerusalem's fall. In 1 Chronicles 24, the nineteenth lot names one course among twenty-four into which David divided the priesthood, an ordinary administrative number given the same careful record as every other course — nothing in the temple's service was left to informal arrangement. The historical books use the same ordinal to nail down the darkest date in Judah's history with precision: the nineteenth year of king Nebuchadnezzar is when the temple itself was burned and the wall of Jerusalem broken down, an event 2 Kings and Jeremiah both date to the exact year, precisely because God's judgments, like His administrative order for worship, are not vague.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from NINETEEN: the ordinal number; next after the eighteenth, and before the twentieth.
webster_full: NINETEEN, a. Nine and ten; the number consisting of one ten and nine units.
NINETEENTH, a. The ordinal of nineteen; next in order after the eighteenth.
Used of the nineteenth course of Levitical service, one among twenty-four (1 Chronicles).
Used historically to date the fall of Jerusalem to Nebuchadnezzar's nineteenth regnal year (2 Kings, Jeremiah).
Scripture's precision with ordinal numbers reflects a broader biblical conviction that God's dealings, in worship and in judgment, are exact, not approximate.
scriptures: The nineteenth to Pethahiah, the twentieth to Jehezekel,

And in the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month, which is the nineteenth year of king Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, came Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, a servant of the king of Babylon, unto Jerusalem:

Now in the fifth month, in the tenth day of the month, which was the nineteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, came Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, which served the king of Babylon, into Jerusalem,
corruption_summary: Historical-critical skepticism toward the small date discrepancy between 2 Kings 25:8 (seventh day) and Jeremiah 52:12 (tenth day) treats the difference as proof of unreliable transmission rather than the ordinary variation of two independent, complementary eyewitness-based records.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical scholarship sometimes uses minor numerical variants like this three-day difference to cast doubt on the historicity of the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem as a whole. Both texts agree on the nineteenth year, the month, and the essential events; the small variance is consistent with ordinary ancient record-keeping (arrival versus the start of burning, for instance) rather than contradiction.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture's minor textual variants across parallel accounts do not undermine its substantial historical reliability, any more than two honest witnesses' slightly differing details undermine a true report.
roots_summary: The Hebrew ordinal behind nineteenth, tesha-esreh, is built transparently from nine (tesha) and ten (esreh), the same additive pattern behind all the Hebrew teens.
roots_lines: Nineteenth in 1 Chronicles names one of twenty-four carefully ordered courses of priestly service.
Nineteenth in 2 Kings and Jeremiah dates the burning of the temple with historical precision.
The small day-count variance between the two accounts reflects complementary record-keeping, not contradiction.
The Hebrew ordinal is built transparently from nine plus ten.
Scripture's care with ordinal numbers reflects its broader conviction that God's dealings are exact.
usage: The nineteenth to Pethahiah — one course among twenty-four in David's ordering of the priesthood.
The nineteenth year of king Nebuchadnezzar — the precisely dated fall and burning of Jerusalem.
Complementary dating in 2 Kings and Jeremiah — two records of the same catastrophic year.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon nigontyne, nine + ten — the cardinal number one less than twenty.
biblical_def:
Nahor lived after he begat Terah an hundred and nineteen years. Nineteen cities with their villages. There lacked of David's servants nineteen men and Asahel.

Nineteen appears sparingly and plainly: a patriarch's remaining years, a tally of Israelite towns, a battlefield count of the dead. Nahor's hundred and nineteen years after Terah's birth belongs to the long genealogical bridge of Genesis 11, the ages shortening generation by generation as the narrative moves from the flood toward Abraham, a quiet witness to a world running down under the curse even as covenant promise approaches. Joshua's nineteen cities are Naphtali's territorial inheritance recorded with the same bureaucratic exactness given to every tribe, the conquest of Canaan reduced, on the page, to careful lists rather than only battle narrative. And 2 Samuel's nineteen men and Asahel is the grim ledger of civil war's cost after Abner's forces are routed — Asahel named separately and mourned specially, because Joab's brother's death here will drive the blood-vengeance that shapes the rest of the book.

Scripture's plain use of round numerals in genealogy, land, and war alike reflects its historical, not merely symbolic, intent in these records.

corruption_summary: Skeptical treatments of the Genesis genealogies as symbolic or legendary numbers, rather than historical records, remove the very literalism the text itself presents them with.
corruption_paragraphs: Reading Genesis 11's ages as folkloric rather than historical detaches the genealogy from its stated purpose: a real chain of descent from Shem to Abraham, underwriting the historical particularity of the covenant promises that follow.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Genesis presents these as real lifespans of real ancestors, the declining numbers themselves a witness to the curse's ongoing effect even within the line of promise.
roots_summary: Joshua 19:38's nineteen cities belongs to the tribal allotment formula repeated throughout Joshua 13-19, each tribe's territory recorded by exact town-count as legal land grant, not folklore.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon hundeahtatig, eight tens — the cardinal number equal to four twenties; usually rendered fourscore in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def:
Methuselah lived an hundred eighty and seven years, and begat Lamech. Methuselah lived after he begat Lamech seven hundred eighty and two years. Lamech lived an hundred eighty and two years, and begat a son.

Eighty, spelled out plainly rather than rendered fourscore as the King James translators usually preferred, appears only within the antediluvian genealogy of Genesis 5, folded into the compound ages of Methuselah and Lamech. Methuselah's hundred eighty and seven years marks the point in his nine hundred sixty-nine-year life when Lamech is born, and his own further seven hundred eighty and two years afterward brings his death, by the standard reckoning, in the very year of the flood — the oldest man who ever lived dying at the threshold of the judgment that would end the world he had witnessed almost from the beginning. Lamech's own hundred eighty and two years before Noah's birth completes the same chapter's careful count, three lives interlocking in a single genealogical line running straight from Adam's fall to the ark.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from EIGHT and TY: the cardinal number consisting of eight tens; usually written fourscore in the Authorized Version.
webster_full: EIGHTY, a. Eight times ten; fourscore.

Used exclusively in Scripture, in this spelled form, for the antediluvian genealogy of Methuselah and Lamech.
Contrast with fourscore, the ordinary Authorized Version rendering, as at Luke 2:37 and Exodus 7:7.
The genealogy's careful count situates Methuselah's death at the threshold of the flood by standard reckoning.

corruption_summary: Skeptical readings dismiss the great ages of Genesis 5 as mythical exaggeration; the confessional reading takes the ages as literal history, part of the same historical narrative that grounds the fall, the flood, and the promised Seed.
corruption_paragraphs: Comparative-mythology approaches treat Methuselah's nine hundred sixty-nine years alongside inflated king-lists from other ancient Near Eastern cultures, implying the numbers are legendary convention rather than history. Genesis presents the ages with the same plain, historical register as every other genealogical detail in the chapter, including the eighty-year markers within them.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the long antediluvian lifespans, whatever physiological explanation one holds for the pre-flood world, are presented by the text as literal history, not folklore, and the line they trace runs directly to Noah and the ark.
roots_summary: The Hebrew behind eighty, shemonim, is the plural form of eight (shemoneh), the ordinary multiplicative pattern for Hebrew tens.
